t: #3610 Minimum Number of Primes to Sum to Target
o: Unbounded coin-change: coins are the first m primes, minimize coin count to hit exactly n, or −1. Example: n=10, m=2 (coins 2,3) → 4 coins (2+2+3+3); n=15, m=5 → 3 coins (5+5+5); n=7, m=6 → 1 coin. Primes larger than n can never be used, so sieving up to n suffices regardless of m.
k: Any prime > n is useless, so sieve primes up to min over the n-th prime bound and cap the list at m coins.
Classic unbounded-knapsack DP: dp[s] = fewest primes summing to s, transition dp[s] = min(dp[s−p]) + 1.

a.i: dp[0] = 0 and dp[s] = 1 + min over usable primes p ≤ s of dp[s − p]. Iterating sums outer and primes inner gives the unbounded (reuse allowed) semantics automatically.
s: Sieve primes up to n; truncate to the first m.
For each s from 1 to n, relax with every prime p ≤ s.
a.t: O(n·π(n)) ≈ O(n²/log n) — for each sum we scan primes up to it.
a.sp: O(n) for the sieve and dp array.

a.i: Treat sums as graph nodes with edges s → s+p weighted 1; BFS from 0 explores sums in increasing coin count, so the first time n is reached gives the minimum. Equivalent complexity but often terminates early for reachable targets.
s: Pop s; for each prime p, if s+p ≤ n and unseen, mark distance and enqueue.
a.t: O(n·π(n)) worst case — each sum enqueued once, scanning primes per pop.

w: Both are standard; the DP is easier to justify, BFS can exit early. Key pitfall: forgetting that primes exceeding n are dead weight (also handles m larger than π(n)). Note some targets (like small odd numbers with only coin 2 available) are unreachable → −1. Follow-up: count the number of minimum-length representations.
